articles.headline: China exile-turned-GOP nominee warns socialist surge could give Beijing greater influence in Washington
keyFacts: Republican congressional nominee Lily Tang Williams warned that Democratic control of Congress could expand Beijing's influence and threaten U.S. national security.
Williams claimed that Democratic immigration policies and a growing socialist surge within the party could allow Chinese intelligence operatives to enter the United States.
Goodlander, the Democratic Socialists of America, and the Democratic Party did not respond to requests for comment.
body: A congressional nominee who escaped communist China after the Tiananmen Square massacre warned that a Democratic-controlled Congress could create opportunities for Beijing to expand its influence in Washington, threatening U.S. national security.

Lily Tang Williams, the Republican nominee for New Hampshire's 2nd Congressional District, told Fox News Digital that China, a country she believes "wants to bring down the United States," would capitalize on "America’s weakness" if Congress were to be controlled by Democrats in January.

"I fear that the country I love is becoming the country I left," Williams, who is challenging Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H., told Fox News Digital. "China will be very happy to see Democrats control the House and Senate. The Democrats want open borders, they want to defund police and abolish private property. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is looking at this as good news."
CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE

Williams pointed to a recent Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) trip, claiming that more than a dozen high-ranking members of the organization traveled to China to "produce favorable coverage of China and its regime," as an example of the Chinese government taking advantage of the "vulnerable Democratic Party" to promote itself in the U.S.
"They now share a similar ideology," Williams said.
DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA NEED TO ACTUALLY MEET THE CHINA THEY CLAIM TO LOVE

Williams also argued that Democrats' immigration policies could make it easier for Chinese intelligence operatives to enter the U.S., warning about the potential for espionage along the southern border.

The candidate said she believes the DSA's growing influence within the Democratic Party could shape congressional decisions even if Democrats remain in the minority or more moderate lawmakers hold leadership positions.

"The Democrat Party is hijacked by the DSA," Williams said. "We’re going to have a DSA-run Congress, whether moderate Democrats like it or not. Moderate Democrat voters are still so complacent. They don't come out and condemn this extremism because they may even be afraid of repercussions from the DSA and DSA voters."
A recent Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans have a positive view of socialism, for the first time since 2010.

Williams pointed to the rise of socialism among Americans and the possibility that at least six new DSA-affiliated lawmakers could enter Congress in January as reasons for concern about the direction of the Democratic Party.
"Congress will be controlled by people who sympathize with the CCP and its Marxist principles," Williams warned.
TOP DEM TORCHES SOCIALISTS TAKING OVER HIS PARTY: 'THEY'RE ANTI-AMERICAN'

Williams also criticized her Democratic opponent and other members of the party for what she described as their refusal to condemn Marxism, arguing that moderate Democrats could increasingly side with the party's progressive wing in the 120th Congress.

"Our country could fall from within, because we don't really have a good policy to protect ourselves and our national security," Williams said. "My opponent refuses to condemn Marxism and Marxist American figures like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when asked. This is very troubling."

During her phone interview with Fox News Digital, Williams raised concerns that lawmakers sympathetic to Marxist ideology could pose national security risks if they gained access to sensitive or classified information.
Goodlander, the DSA and the Democratic Party did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

articles.headline: Spain train crash caused by operator 'inexplicably' telling driver to resume journey despite red signal, transport minister says
keyFacts: At least 64 people died and dozens were injured after two high-speed trains collided near Toledo, Spain.
Spain's transport minister Oscar Puente stated that one train was inexplicably told to resume its journey despite a red signal.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and King Felipe VI altered their schedules to travel to the crash site and monitor the emergency response.
body: What you need to know
- At least 64 people have died after two high-speed trains collided near Toledo
- The crash has caused at least 50 injuries
- Spain's transport minister Oscar Puente says one of the trains was told to continue its journey even though all trains on the track had been ordered to stop
- Authorities say more than 500 people were on board the two trains
Here are the latest updates from the high-speed train crash in Spain on Wednesday, October 28:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Renfe train was told to continue journey despite red signal, transport minister says

The Renfe high-speed train that crashed into another stationary train had been told to continue its journey "as normal" despite the fact that all trains on the section of track in Toledo province had been told to stop, Spain's Transport Minister Oscar Puente has said.
Puente told a press conference at the ADIF control center in Madrid that the control system at the train station in Urda had failed due to a computer error.
That failure meant that a 63-kilometer section of track had no control system, which triggered an automatic stop, or "red signal," for all rail traffic on the parts of the track affected.
Operators at the control center ADIF, the company that is responsible for managing and maintaining Spain's railway infrastructure, took over communications.
"At 8:36 a.m. the Renfe train was told to resume its journey 'with normality'," Puente explained, a decision he described as "inexplicable."
He said that between that time and the moment of impact at 8:53, the Renfe train had traveled about 25 kilometers (15.5 miles), likely reaching a speed of over 100 kilometers (60 miles) per hour.

During the press conference, Puente refused to respond to questions about whether he would resign in the wake of the crash, saying his attention was on clarifying the circumstances that led to the crash and supporting the victims.
EU leaders send condolences, support to Spain after crash
Senior European Union leaders Ursula von der Leyen and Kaja Kallas have sent their condolences to the victims of the high-speed rail crash and their families.
European Commission President von der Leyen said "Europe mourns with you."
Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy and security chief, said she had spoken to Spain's Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares to convey her "profound condolences following the tragic accident."
"Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives. I wish a swift recovery to the injured and strength to all those affected," Kallas said.
European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho, meanwhile, said the bloc was "ready to help Spain if needed."
Spain's PM Sanchez heading to crash site
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is traveling to Urda, where two high-speed trains collided.
At least 64 people have been killed, while more than 80 people have been injured in one of the worst rail accidents in Spain's history.

In a post on X, the Moncloa Palace, the prime minister's official residence, said Sanchez was heading to Urda to "support the work of the emergency teams and to convey his support to those affected and their families."
"The priority is to attend to the victims and ensure the maximum coordination between administrations," it added.
Spanish royals 'saddened and distressed' over accident
Spain's royal family has issued a statement following the deadly train crash in Toledo.
In a post on X, the royals said they are "deeply saddened and distressed" over the accident.
"We share the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt thoughts to the injured and everyone affected."

Spain's King Felipe VI, meanwhile, told reporters in Valencia that he was cutting short his military training exercise at the Jaime I Military Base to return to Madrid to monitor the emergency response to the accident.
Felipe added that he had already been in touch with the regional Castilla-La Mancha president.
Do we know what caused the accident?
A train operated by the private Iryo consortium was reportedly told to stop by rail infrastructure manager ADIF due to a faulty signal, a person briefed on the disaster told the Reuters news agency.
Government officials have not confirmed what caused the train crash, and neither Renfe nor Iryo have commented on the cause.

DW has spoken to Nick Kingsley, the executive editor of the Railway Gazette International, about what might have caused the crash, the second fatal accident to hit Spain's high-speed rail network this year.
Kingsley described it as "a dark day for the Spanish rail industry" and said there would be "profound questions asked" as to how this accident occurred.

While he cautioned that it was still too early to speculate, Kingsley said: "The key point with high-speed railway is you design safety systems and especially signalling and train control systems such that the trains do not crash. This should never happen."
He said investigators would be looking into whether there are any similarities with the fatal accident in January.

"The fact that these two accidents happened in the same year when we had 30+ years without a single fatal accident on a high-speed rail network anywhere in the world, to now have this happen twice in one year in the same country is quite shocking," Kingsley told DW.
What are investigators going to be looking at?
"If reports that one crashed into the back of the other are confirmed, that will raise questions about the protection of those sections of track," Kingsley said.

He explained that the "fundamental principle of railway operation is that you have a signalling system that is designed to prevent two trains from occupying the same section of track. This is a fundamental tenet of railway operation."
Kingsley added that it will take a long time, possibly several weeks or even months, "to establish a definitive sequence of events."
Death toll climbs to 64 — regional government
The death toll from the accident has risen to at least 64, a spokesperson for Castilla-La Mancha's regional president, Emiliano Garcia-Page, has said.
At least 58 people were injured, many of them seriously, officials have confirmed.
The toll has risen several times during the day, with the possibility remaining that it could still go up.
Regional president: 'We expect more deaths'

The president of the regional Castilla-La Mancha government, Emiliano Garcia-Page, has told reporters at the scene of the accident that at least 80 people were lightly or moderately injured as a result of the crash.
"There are also fewer who were seriously injured, so we unfortunately do expect more deaths," Garcia-Page said.
He added that the priority is to treat the injured and move them to hospital.
"We are in the heart of the emergency, so the priority is to attend to the injured, the dead and the victims' families," he said.
Help is arriving from neighboring regions, the president said, as he urged people to remain calm and to allow the emergency services to deal with the accident.
He also refused to speculate on what caused the accident.
"I'm not the one who should comment on the causes, that should come from judicial authorities. The judicial authorities should be the ones to establish the causes of this incident," he said.
Spain reels from latest serious train accident
The collision in Toledo on Wednesday morning comes just months after another devastating rail disaster near Adamuz in Andalusia in January.
In that accident, a high-speed train derailed and collided with an oncoming train, killing 46 people and injuring more than 150.
The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.
IN PICTURES: Spain high-speed train collision
Spanish PM Sanchez 'shocked' by 'serious train accident'
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said he was "shocked" by the "serious train accident" near Toledo on Wednesday morning.
He said that emergency services were on the scene to assist those affected in coordination with local administrations.
"My affection, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families," he wrote on social media.
Minister: 'We are expecting this to be a major tragedy'
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia confirmed that Wednesday's train crash was a "high-speed impact."
She said it was too soon to confirm a final casualty figure but told local broadcaster TVE: "We are expecting this to be a major tragedy."
Spain train crash: what do we know?
Images from the scene showed at least two severely damaged train carriages flipped over on their side after tumbling down an embankment.

One of the trains, operated by AVE, was reportedly carrying 397 passengers while the other, operated by IRYO, had 146 people on board, according to the Castilla-La Mancha local government spokeswoman.
A reporter for local broadcaster TVE described scenes of "absolute chaos" and a constant stream of ambulances and emergency vehicles.
The El Pais newspaper cited witnesses describing numerous injuries and  emergency medical teams arriving at the scene.

"All resources are currently being deployed," spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told the AFP news agency, including "several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units."
In a post on social media, rail operator Adif confirmed that "traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed rail line has been suspended following a rear-end collision between two trains."
Train passenger: 'We heard a massive roar'
A passenger on one of the trains involved in Wednesday's deadly crash has described the moment the collision occured.
"We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds as if the train were about to derail," Miguel told local radio station COPE.
"Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been the other one."
Train collision in Spain kills at least 30, injures many
At least 30 people were killed in a train crash in central Spain on Wednesday morning, authorities told Spanish national news agency EFE.
"The information we are receiving is not good at all," a spokesperson for the government of the Castilla-La Mancha region said.

"There has been a collision between two trains [and] there are injured people," added Manuel Galans, mayor of the town of Urda in the province of Toledo, close to where the incident took place just after 9 a.m. local time.
The mayor of another nearby village, Jesus Perez of Los Yebenes, told Spanish TV that the accident appeared "serious."
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia told national broadcaster TVE that it was a "high impact accident, it will be a major tragedy" but said it was too soon to confirm a final casualty figure.
"We don't just need help from nearby hospitals, we need nearby hospitals that have ICU beds," she added.
Welcome to our coverage
There has been a major accident in central Spain, where a high-speed train have collided with another that had stopped.
At least 30 people have been killed and there are "a significant number" of injured, as officials say that toll is very likely to climb.
Stay tuned as we bring you the latest.

articles.headline: Chiefs reportedly signing Tucker in wake of sexual misconduct allegations as Butker struggles
keyFacts: The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad.
The Ravens previously released Tucker following a slump in form and a 10-game NFL ban for violating the personal conduct policy after massage therapists accused him of inappropriate sexual behavior.
Tucker's signing comes amid a poor start to the season by Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker, who has missed five of his 16 field goal attempts.
body: The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad after Harrison Butker’s poor start to the season.

Tucker was widely considered one of the best kickers in NFL history until the Ravens released him in May 2025. The Ravens said his departure was a “football decision” after a slump in form, but the move came months after he was accused of inappropriate sexual behavior by massage therapists. Tucker denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges but he served a 10-game NFL ban for violating the league’s personal conduct policy.

More than a dozen massage therapists from spas and wellness centers in the Baltimore area accused Tucker of inappropriate sexual behavior. One therapist who spoke to the Baltimore Banner, which broke the story, described Tucker’s alleged behavior as “really degrading”. Another said: “I can’t watch sports anymore. I see his face everywhere.”

The 37-year-old has not played in the NFL since he was released by Baltimore. During his time with the Ravens, he made seven Pro Bowls and won the Super Bowl in his rookie season. His final season in Baltimore, in which he made just 73.3% of his field goals, was statistically the worst of his career. Tucker’s career average for field goals is 89.1%.

Butker, who has won three Super Bowls with the Chiefs, has missed five of his 16 field goal attempts this season. The 31-year-old Butker has also been involved in off-field controversy. During a commencement address at Benedictine College in 2024, he criticized Pride month, working women, Joe Biden’s leadership during the Covid-19 pandemic and abortion.

“I think it is you, the women, who have had the most diabolic lies told to you,” Butker said during the speech. “Some of you may go on to lead successful careers in the world, but I would venture to guess that the majority of you are most excited about your marriage and the children you will bring into this world. I can tell you that my beautiful wife Isabelle would be the first to say her life truly started when she started living her vocation as a wife and as a mother.”

articles.headline: How big should Democrats go on childcare? We asked a potential 2028 contender.
keyFacts: Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear told Vox that Congress should take action to ensure every state provides universal pre-K for four-year-olds.
Beshear launched Kentucky pre-K pilot programs using federal workforce funds after state Republican leadership blocked budget funding.
Beshear stated that federal childcare investments can increase workforce participation and tax revenue to help address national debt.
body: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who is weighing a presidential run, told Vox that he believes Congress “should take action to make sure that every state provides pre-K for 4-year-olds.” | KC McGinnis/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The midterms are racing to their conclusion, but the presidential contest is right around the corner. As the next primaries begin to take shape, how Democratic hopefuls intend to address childcare is already shaping up to be a major question.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who is weighing a run for president , is one of the potential contenders with hands-on experience around this issue. Facing Republican opposition in the state legislature, he recently redirected federal funds to launch a pre-K pilot program , standing up 3,000 new seats since May. And he believes national Democrats should be making a push to expand access to preschool as well.

We wanted to better understand not only how Beshear is thinking about early childhood initiatives, but also his approach to spending on new federal programs more broadly, and what he’s learned from past efforts to expand access to families that failed. On Tuesday, we spoke with Beshear remotely about his work in the state — and his message to Democrats outside of it. Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

Since 1991, Kentucky has supported voluntary preschool, yet today still only about a quarter of 4-year-olds can attend the state-funded program. Why has it been so hard to make preschool available to every family who wants it?

Well, it shouldn’t be hard. You know, pre-K is an opportunity for every child to get off to a good start. And right now in Kentucky, because of the history you just mentioned, over half of our Kentucky children show up not ready for kindergarten. So before they’ve ever walked into a public school they are already behind.
So why has it been hard to make that happen?

Well, so at least in my tenure, somehow pre-K has become political. You know, 4-year-olds aren’t registered to vote. They’re not Democrats or Republicans. But I’ve pushed every year to get this in the budget. We can easily fund it given that I’ve produced a surplus every year I’ve been governor, yet our Republican leadership simply will not let it happen.
So, as you mentioned, there have been attempts at expanding this before. What have you learned from those earlier attempts, and what are you doing differently now?

So it’s interesting you bring that up. The same leadership that will not pass pre-K funding in our current budget cycle voted for it under the last Republican governor, but won’t vote for it under me. The last Republican governor vetoed the expansion , and they expressed their displeasure. So the only thing that’s changed here is the party of the person in charge. And what I hear is our Republican leadership saying they don’t want to give me a win, but they’re willing to hand a loss to all of these 4-year olds.

But for me as governor, I don’t get to accept excuses. So what I’ve done is I’ve taken flexible workforce training funds called WIOA funds , which you can use for a lot of different things. They’re used in a number of states for pre-K. And we have launched five pilot programs in different parts of the Commonwealth that are already a stunning success.

The smallest county in Kentucky is called Robertson County and has zero childcare. You have to drive 40 minutes one way or an hour another way just for any form of child care. It’s one of the places we started this and just to see the parents and the impact that it has on them — most of those parents don’t share my political party — but this is a great opportunity for them that they’re embracing.
It sounds like it’s gotten pretty polarized in your state. When you talk with Republican lawmakers privately, what do they tell you about why they won’t support expanded preschool?

Well, many rank-and-file Republicans in our state legislature want pre-K, and a number of them helped us to push for it this time. But leadership that’s been here for far too long and gotten far too partisan is simply blocking it at this point. What we need is for it to get to a vote, because this is the top polling education issue among Republicans. Again, because it’s not political.

If we had ballot measures and we put this on there, it would pass 80-plus percent because everyone wants that opportunity for their children. My hope is now that we have started these pilot programs, including one in Franklin County, which is where the seat of government is, that they can go and see how good this program is and not allow the next set of 4-year-olds or the next set of 4-year-olds or the next set of 4-year-olds to miss out on it. But I’m gonna do everything I can with the funding that I can find to provide as much of this opportunity as possible.

So there’s a lot of speculation about whether you might run for president. Without asking you to make any announcements here, I wanted to ask how you’re thinking about these issues nationally. You recently called yourself a more “practical” candidate when explaining your concerns about Medicare-for-all. When you look at something like childcare or pre-K from a federal perspective, what does being practical mean?

I think it means that there is a role for the federal government, and I’m supporting a number of congressional candidates right now and talking to all of them about pre-K. When people talk about the different sides of the Democratic Party — which I think is an overblown story, but still — like when Elizabeth Warren and I get together, we try to find some different things that we both agree on that we could work together on, and pre-K is one of those areas, so is housing.
“I do believe that Congress should take action to make sure that every state provides pre-K for 4-year-olds.”

I do believe that Congress should take action to make sure that every state provides pre-K for 4-year-olds. That’d be something that would be good for the United States that could actually bring Democrats and Republicans together and lift up people in all 50 states. And wouldn’t that be nice? To do something that is the right thing, that is the smart thing, and to do it in a nonpartisan way.
I know you mentioned pre-K for 4-year-olds. What do you think parents should be able to count on from the government before their kids turn four?

I believe that there is a role for government in childcare, and we’re working on it right now in Kentucky. We launched our first childcare center for state employees, and we’re learning a lot from it. Now I admit that the child care challenge is complex. You know, we have private childcare, we have public childcare, we have nonprofit childcare, and making sure we can get in and understand the real cost drivers of that.

What we would do as a state, or what the federal government could do, is develop an effective understanding of all those different parts and pieces. But just pre-K could put 70,000 more people into our workforce in Kentucky, so think about what better childcare could do to the workforce in our country. And it’s something that we could afford because we would see more dollars coming back in terms of tax revenue from that many more people in the workforce than we would ever pay out in child care.

Representative Ro Khanna recently proposed a federal program that would cover childcare costs for nearly all families with kids under age six, including care by relatives and neighbors, and offer a thousand dollar a month to parents who stay home with children under three. Would you support that kind of program?

Yeah, I haven’t seen the details of it. I think that that would present some real challenges with our current system as it is. What I would see is getting into the complexities of each of the forms of child care and how we can augment it, how we can build out on the system that we have right now, but also to address those child care deserts that I’m not sure this plan would fix. I mean, we’ve got counties that have no options — public, private or nonprofit.

And so I agree that it’s a challenge. I think it’s going to take us being both surgical on the micro and adopting policies on the macro. And I believe it probably won’t all happen at once, even though that sounds great. It’s how do we make improvement after improvement after improvement and expand and expand more as we understand the underlying mechanics better.

When I talk to people about why childcare and universal pre-K fell out of Joe Biden’s Build Back Better agenda, some say that Democrats tried to do too much and that they needed to narrow their agenda and prioritize specific issues more. Others, like Senator Elizabeth Warren, say that Democrats didn’t fight hard enough for child care, for universal pre-K.
What lessons do you take from the last federal child care push?

The federal government has to act with more urgency. We get in a lot of these debates about whether a plan is perfect or if a plan’s only 80 percent perfect. Listen, take the 80 percent and start working it. Provide the American people with some help which they need.

Now, the Biden administration could have had an imperfect plan. But if they’d implemented that imperfect plan, there would be more childcare options right now. And I admit as a governor, I’m practical. You know, getting stuff done is incredibly important. I want to provide relief to all families, but if I can provide relief to a lot of families, let’s start there and then let’s get bigger.
Just to clarify that, what would you have done differently? What would it look like if you had been part of the conversation?
“If it were me, I would push for universal pre-K for 4-year-olds immediately. That is the immediate relief that takes 25 percent of that burden off of working parents.”

If it were me, I would push for universal pre-K for 4-year-olds immediately. That is the immediate relief that takes 25 percent of that burden off of working parents and then I’d work on a bill that addresses childcare, that makes sure that we have all the stakeholders at the table.

Something that I hear in DC while reporting on childcare is that Democrats in Congress are working to make big new plans for 2027 and 2028. But we know they’d also face real pressure to restore things like the billions cut in Medicaid funding.
As you think about the future, where does childcare or universal pre-K fall on your list of priorities?

It’s high on the list of priorities because my priorities are the American people, their well-being, and the ability to chase that American dream. Right? That American dream is about having a job where you can support your family, being able to see a doctor when you’re sick, driving safe roads and bridges, getting your kids the best education possible, and feeling safe in your community. And so pre-K and childcare falls right there. I believe that.

When Democrats retake Congress or when they retake the presidency, we have got to be laser focused on people’s lives and how hard they are right now, but also do it in a smart way that increases the size of our workforce when there are people that want to go back to work, but simply can’t afford to because of the cost of childcare or a lack of those education options.
You recently praised Bill Clinton for running a budget surplus. Do you think that bringing down the deficit should be a priority for the next Democratic president?

Yes, and and I believe that you can and should run a surplus in that job. Now I think what you do is you grow the economy and that helps you pay for those services, but you’ve got to be careful about new spending. That doesn’t mean that you don’t engage in it because there are some things that you could spend on, I believe, like childcare and pre-K that would result in more federal revenue coming in that would allow you to run that surplus. But over time, we’ve got to start addressing the national debt.
Did the Biden administration’s experience with inflation change your thinking about how much the federal government should spend?

Well, I believe the Biden administration was attempting to get us out of the recession that was Covid. Now you saw a huge recession in Covid, and they put these policies in place that shot us out of that recession faster than anyone ever thought was possible, but it probably overshot that target. I think we should have been communicating to the American people about how we had gotten our economy back on track in record time, but it had gone a little too far, and that we were going to make it through. That could have even been a patriotic call because I believe it was a patriotic time. You know, defeating a pandemic that came to kill as many of us as possible.

You’ve talked in this conversation and elsewhere about being pragmatic, acting with urgency, not being overly ideological. A lot of Democrats today make the case now that the pragmatic thing to do is to go big on new programs, push for universal childcare, push for universal health care, abandon these half measures and incremental steps.
I’d love to hear you talk about that. Is that your instinct?

Well, I’d have to see a program that would actually work. You know, it’s great to talk about a massive program, but then you’ve got to get down in the details, and will it deliver on day one? Or will it crash a system that is imperfect but is delivering to a degree and could deliver more? I’m not against the big idea, but what I’m against is throwing something out there that in the practical real world can’t work.
What role do you see for employers in building out our childcare and early education systems?

I think that employers have a big role to play. And I see families where an employer has childcare, excited to go to work, knowing their kid is in the building or or close by, the convenience that that provides. They can go down and have lunch with their kids, which is something that I’ve missed out on in my work life. so I think it is critical.

What we’ve seen in Kentucky is our large employers, we can work with them on it and we can get it done, but it’s midsized employers that we have to rise to that challenge. You know, places that only have a couple hundred employees, or maybe even 12 or 15, how we can band together for those businesses to be able to provide it. And I believe the federal government should be working directly with those companies, because we’ve got to make the economics work. The federal government, in coordination with those employers, could get this right, create a lot more slots, and help people get back to work.

articles.headline: Microsoft faces potential vote: Shareholders curious about its plans to tackle emissions
keyFacts: Trillium Asset Management is backing a shareholder proposal asking Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas emission targets.
Microsoft reported that its emissions increased from 13 million tons of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025 due to AI datacenter expansion.
Microsoft recommended that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing that existing sustainability reporting and established frameworks are sufficient.
body: Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting.

The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020 , aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050.

But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in.
Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase.

This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO 2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025.
However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons.

The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024.

Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8.

In an SEC filing , the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually.

The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan.

It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt.

In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. If Microsoft is in danger of failing to meet its 2030 commitments, it could suffer reputational harm, and the filing claims it is already the subject of legal action by investors alleging insufficient disclosure of its AI and cloud spending.

On the flip side, it says that disclosure of a climate transition plan will likely prove valuable to large institutional investors who view climate change as a systemic risk to future economic growth.

We asked Microsoft for comment, but it already recommended in another SEC filing that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing it fails to show that Microsoft’s existing disclosures are insufficient for investors to assess its climate-related strategy and performance.

Instead, the firm says that the proposal requests a collection of new disclosures that go beyond not just legal and regulatory requirements, but also established voluntary climate-reporting frameworks.

The proposal seeks hypothetical scenarios, contingency plans and other forward-looking information that is inherently uncertain and subject to change, Microsoft states, saying it will remain focused on its Sustainability Report and other environmental reporting while meeting any new disclosure mandates that may arise globally. ®

articles.headline: Dexter: Resurrection Season 2 Premiere Review
keyFacts: Dexter: Resurrection Season 2 premieres on Paramount+ with the Premium Plan on Friday, October 30, with the first episode titled "Risky Business."
The premiere episode introduces an antsy Dexter experiencing midlife recklessness alongside a few new villains played by Brian Cox and Dan Stevens.
The episode also follows Harrison working as an NYPD rookie while Detective Wallace takes notice of his new career.
body: This is a non-spoiler review for the Dexter: Resurrection Season 2 premiere, "Risky Business," which airs on Paramount+ with the Premium Plan on Friday, October 30.
Uh oh, Dexter's got that itch again. The itch to kill? Nah, that never went away. I'm talking about the more frustrating itch. The midlife crisis urge to be reckless.

In the first episode of Dexter: Resurrection's second season -- which I really wish had just been given a whole new subtitle -- the Bay Harbor Butcher (Michael C. Hall) is feeling a little under-appreciated for what he believes are his life-saving endeavors, and he might be looking for a spotlight of gratitude (think of the parade he imagined for himself at the end of the very first season). "Risky Business" makes for a good start to this new batch of episodes, introducing both an ansty protagonist and a few new Big Bads to contend with. Of course, one episode only gives us a small glimpse into the upcoming season and it's not enough to fully judge what's ahead, but if Dexter's "I'm over 50 now" inner turmoil and restlessness are treated differently than his past bouts of self-reflection and unease, Season 2 could be a very interesting take.

To quickly recap the journey of the series: Seasons 1 through 4 of the original show were groundbreaking. Seasons 5 through 8 were uneven, and at their worst had really bad creative turns. Dexter: New Blood was good, and landed very well as a revised ending for the saga. Resurrection, while initially eliciting eye rolls because of the titular resurrection, wound up being a true return to form for the series, feeling the most like the early seasons of the first show.

One thing that remains true though, Dexter-wise, is that the story stumbles when Dexter doesn't learn from his mistakes. Sure, he's flawed and driven by a mad desire to spill blood. He stretches himself too thin and will also kill an innocent person in a pinch in order to escape capture. There's also a self-destructive element to him that we accept. It's enticing. What we don't want is him to be a bonehead who resets anew every season. So far, in the wake of "Risky Business," we're safe. After dealing with Peter Dinklage's Leon Prater and his gruesome gallery of both murderous memorabilia and actual maniacs in Resurrection Season 1, Dex has realized that he's a big deal. Too big to be toiling away as a ride share driver, for sure, and maybe even too big to let poor James Doakes (Erik King) go down as the Butcher. Perhaps things need to get a bit more... public.

'Risky Business' makes for a good start to this new batch of episodes, introducing both an ansty protagonist and a few new Big Bads to contend with. While Dexter is busy feeling time's encroaching talons, we catch up with Harrison (Jack Alcott), keeping the Morgan family cop tradition alive as an NYPD rookie. How will Harrison deal with his dad pushing things to the edge? Ultimately, where will his loyalties lie, once again, if push comes to shove and Dexter starts kicking up dirt? Because there's darkness on the horizon. Not only is wise Detective Wallace (Kadia Saraf) still around, and taking notice of Harrison's new career, but madmen like the New York Ripper (Wallace's white whale from last season) and the hot-off-the-presses Five Borough Killer are making things super slicey and dicey out there. Fun casting alert for those two, by the way, with "first-ever on-screen Hannibal Lecter" Brian Cox as the Ripper and a stoic, menacing Dan Stevens as FBK.

The juice of "Risky Business" involves Dexter tying up Prater's loose ends, which means Eric Stonestreet's Al Walker returns to get some more time in the sun. Here, Stonestreet shows a much more dangerous, horrifying side to his Rapunzel killer, playing even more against his Modern Family persona. I won't go into any more guest star/adversary/obstacle details than what I've already divulged, but "Risky Business" plays well, sets the table nicely, and even has some inspired '80s punk rock needle drops.

articles.headline: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
keyFacts: Researchers reported that declining Antarctic sea ice since 2016 caused a sharp salinity increase in a vast deep layer of the Southern Ocean.
Co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen stated that this salty layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward and transports heat, carbon, and nutrients globally.
Gayen noted that more monitoring is needed because these ocean changes could produce global impacts within five years.
body: The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say.

In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years.

The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen, a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India.

Gayen said the study combined six independent datasets to track changes in the Southern Ocean from 2004 to 2024. The data came from Argo floats, which drift through the ocean and periodically descend to different depths to measure water properties such as density and salinity, then resurface to transmit the readings. A 2025 study also detected increasing surface salinity linked to declining sea ice, he added.

Antarctic sea ice reached its highest extent in the satellite record in 2014 and suddenly dropped to a record low just two years later. The sea ice remained well below the 2014 extent and reached another low point in 2023, when it measured about 1 million square miles below the 1981 to 2010 average, with an area of ice about four times the size of Texas gone. As the ice dwindles, there’s less freshwater available during the melt season, making the Antarctic Intermediate Water saltier.

Changes to the density, thickness and salinity of the layer influence how heat moves between the surface of the ocean and deeper waters, which “could affect how the ocean stores and redistributes heat,” Gayen said. More monitoring is needed to track the changes, he added, because impacts are potentially “knocking on your door” within five years.

articles.headline: FCC clears Amazon Leo to acquire mobile-satellite operator Globalstar
keyFacts: The US Federal Communications Commission approved Amazon Leo's 11.5 billion dollar acquisition of mobile-satellite operator Globalstar.
The deal is designed to expand Amazon Leo's space-based footprint and allow direct-to-device service.
The FCC said the deal is likely to benefit the public by enhancing data coverage in underserved areas.
body: FCC clears Amazon Leo to acquire mobile-satellite operator Globalstar
The deal is designed to allow Leo to to deliver direct-to-device service.

Amazon Leo's $11.5 billion acquisition of mobile-satellite operator Globalstar has been approved by the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the regulator announced. The deal is designed to expand Leo's space-based footprint and allow direct-to-device service for its growing satellite network, Amazon previously said.

"The companies' complementary assets promise to enhance Amazon Leo's entry into the direct-to-device segment and create a stronger satellite operator capable of offering fixed and mobile services to residential, business, and government customers," the FCC wrote in a press release that echoed Amazon's own talking points. The regulator said that the deal is likely to benefit the public by enhancing data coverage in underserved areas.

You may not know Globalstar but have possibly used its services, as the company provides Apple's emergency satellite connectivity for compatible iPhones and Watches. Interestingly, Apple also held a 20 percent stake in Globalstar prior to its takeover. As part of the deal, Leo will power satellite services for supported iPhone and Apple Watch models.

Leo, a rival to SpaceX's Starlink, has been active of late. The company recently announced that it has 400 satellites in orbit and revealed last month that it had launched high-quality satellite internet service in Uzbekistan. It's teaming up with Delta to eventually bring satellite internet to flights, as well. Amazon recently added six new Arianespace launches and aims to have more than 3,000 low-earth orbit satellites up in the near future, still well short of SpaceX's 11,000 satellites.

articles.headline: Fox One Will Track 2026 Midterm Election Results With New App Experience
keyFacts: Fox unveiled a new interactive election experience for Fox One app subscribers to track 2026 midterm results.
The new features include a home screen command center, a curated election hub, and an AI-powered chatbot called Ask Fox.
The new in-app election experience will launch on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3.
body: The 2026 midterm elections are less than a week away, and Fox has unveiled a new interactive experience for Fox One app subscribers on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, to keep up with the news and results as they come in across the country.

With hundreds of House, Senate, gubernatorial and local races happening all at once, it can be tough to follow along with every update. According to a statement, Fox One has launched an interface to keep track of everything, “where a race in one state reframes the math in another and where what matters most to viewers may be a ballot measure in their own county.”

The features that’ll appear as part of this rollout include a command center on the Fox One home screen, with widgets that update in real time on things like voter polls, contest results and Fox News “Election Insights” on key races; a curated election hub that’ll include all of Fox’s election coverage; and a new Elections Mode version of Ask Fox, the app’s AI-powered chatbot, where viewers can ask election-based questions and receive answers in real time.
More from CNET

“The results don’t arrive in order, and no two viewers are following the same set of races,” said Amit Dudakia, senior vice president and head of product at Fox Direct to Consumer. “With Fox One, we’re keeping coverage from Fox News and Fox Stations at the center and building the context around it, so viewers aren’t toggling between a stream and a second screen to understand what just happened.”

Fox One’s complete channel portfolio includes Fox News Channel, Fox Nation, Fox Sports, B1G, FS1, FS2, the Fox Network and local Fox stations. It is available at no additional cost for cable and satellite TV customers and is priced at $20 a month for a stand-alone subscription to the app. The new in-app election experience will launch on Election Day.

articles.headline: 'Relax, I love Kane and Lamine Yamal' - Henry defends his Ballon d'Or hosting
keyFacts: Thierry Henry defended his hosting of the Ballon d'Or ceremony after receiving public criticism for several remarks he made during the event.
Henry addressed backlash over jokes directed at Lamine Yamal, co-host Kate Scott, and overall winner Harry Kane in a social media video.
Henry stated that he respects Lamine Yamal and Kate Scott, explained that Scott was in on the joke, and called Harry Kane a worthy winner.
body: - Published
Thierry Henry has defended himself after criticism over the way he hosted Monday's Ballon d'Or ceremony.

The former France and Arsenal forward, who has come under fire for remarks he made towards Barcelona star Lamine Yamal, overall winner Harry Kane and co-host Kate Scott on the night, has addressed what he said was "people getting really excited about nothing".
Henry, who was presenting the ceremony alongside CBS Sports colleague Scott, joked with Lamine Yamal about him winning a third successive young player of the year award.
He also corrected Scott's pronunciation of Brazil legend Socrates' name and admitted he wanted fellow Frenchman Kylian Mbappe to beat Kane to the top prize.
Addressing the Lamine Yamal situation, which received an audible reaction from the audience in attendance, Henry said he wasn't "checking his ego" and emphasised his admiration of the young Spaniard.
On the night, he teased Lamine Yamal by saying of his young player award: "It's your third one, right? But is it the one you really wanted to win?"
Speaking in a social media video on Wednesday, Henry said: "I'm a big fan of Lamine Yamal. I wasn't checking his ego at all - that you didn't like the joke, I can understand.
"But don't do that, he's one of the players I'd pay to watch, I love him."
The 49-year-old also responded to criticism over his response to co-host Scott's pronunciation of 'Socrates', claiming she was in on the joke herself.
"You didn't like the joke, I understand, but please stop saying I disrespected Kate," Henry said.
"I will never do that and you can ask her, she was on the joke with me. She did Soc on purpose, and I said Soc, so please stop inventing stories."
Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka won the Socrates Award for his humanitarian and charity work.
Henry added Kane was a "worthy winner" of the Ballon d'Or before telling everyone to "relax" after his support of Mbappe's claim to the prize.
"I'm French and I was always going to back up and support my fellow countryman," he said.

"I said to [Kane], 'You are a worthy winner, you deserve it, you are the example that work ethic is a talent, working hard is a talent'. Well done, Harry Kane - and I call him Sir Harry Kane since the World Cup.
"So please, people out there, relax, relax. I love Harry Kane, I love Lamine Yamal and I didn't disrespect Kate. She was on the joke with me."

articles.headline: Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone
keyFacts: Israel's election is too close to call between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot, with final vote tallies expected soon.
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 10,000 infections and nearly 5,000 deaths, according to figures released.
Election officials stated they expect to finish counting votes by tomorrow afternoon to determine the next prime minister.
body: Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories

Midterm ad spending has surpassed a record $11 billion, according to Ad Impact. An NPR analysis found that candidates in four major Senate races spent more than $15 million on fundraising ads in the 2025-26 election cycle. Meanwhile, President Trump has been campaigning in tight races across states like Texas, Mississippi, and Kansas.

- 🎧 Trump has not been sticking with his standard midterm pitch, which includes touting GOP tax cuts and attacking Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. His jokes, including comments about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted's physique, entertain rally crowds but distract from the key issues the median voter cares about, like the economy and gas prices. Midterm turnout is usually low, but the GOP base still supports him, suggesting many MAGA votes are available, Kurtzleben says. But Trump needing to rally votes in very red states indicates a potential problem for his party.

The election in Israel is too close to call after voters turned out in record numbers to decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in office or oust him for an alternative. Netanyahu was in a tight race with his top rival Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff. Final vote tallies may take time, and if no bloc secures a majority, it could take days or weeks for party leaders to form a governing coalition and determine the next prime minister.

- 🎧 Israelis went to bed thinking Eisenkot had the advantage, but by morning, Netanyahu pulled ahead, making the election too close to call, NPR's Daniel Estrin says. Election officials tell NPR that they expect to finish counting votes by tomorrow afternoon. The leading candidate will have six weeks to form a governing coalition, likely competing for support from defectors in each other's camps. Eisenkot could gain the majority of lawmakers' support in parliament, thanks to a strong showing from Arab-led parties eager to see him as prime minister. Eisenkot's camp is hesitant to form a coalition with Arab parties due to mistrust and demonization of Arab political leaders after the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, Estrin says. He adds that both candidates don't have a clear path to a majority coalition.
The Federal Reserve typically combats inflation by raising interest rates. While prices are currently rising faster than average wages, investors don't expect a rate hike at today's meeting.

- 🎧 The Labor Department's latest cost-of-living report shows consumer prices rose 3.7% in September compared to last year. NPR's Scott Horsley says that marks a larger annual increase than the previous month. Fed policymakers raised interest rates in September, but investors believe the central bank will remain low-key ahead of Election Day and may increase rates again in December.

The Ebola outbreak has surpassed 10,000 people infected since its declaration in May, according to the latest figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo. This outbreak has spread faster than any in history. It is also the largest in geographic scope, spanning from Nigeria to Kenya, and is second in death toll with nearly 5,000 deaths. Around one-third of those who have died have been children.
On the ground

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

With Election Day less than a week away, Morning Edition's Michel Martin went to the Midwest to hear from voters about what is important to them this midterm cycle. In Springfield, Ohio, the Trump administration has conducted an aggressive campaign to deport Haitian residents who have been living legally in the country with Temporary Protected Status. The administration revoked TPS for Haitians during Trump's second term. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed has narrowly won the Democratic Senate nomination, a victory for the party's progressive wing. The swing state is important to both parties, which is why Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned for their party's Senate candidate over the weekend.
Hear what voters in these two states had to say:
- 🎧 In Michigan, many voters expressed burnout as they worry about gas prices and healthcare.
- 🎧 Trump's tariffs are hitting Michigan households harder than any other state because many people depend on cross-border trade. But voters affected said the issue isn't so clear-cut.
- 🎧 Winning a statewide office in Michigan without Detroit is challenging, and El-Sayed didn't perform well there in the primary. Some Black Detroiters said they remain skeptical of him.
- 🎧 Some Springfield, Ohio voters said they are voting early because they are angry about the administration's treatment of Haitians.
Follow the reporting on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.

The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.
Life advice

As the holidays approach and appointments and commitments begin to pile up, author Caroline Sylge recommends a "say no" retreat — a day dedicated to figuring out which obligations you want to decline in the coming weeks and months. While it may seem unconventional to devote an entire day to saying no, this approach can help create space for what truly matters to you. Sylge shared with Life Kit her suggested schedule for a "say no" retreat:
- 🙅 As soon as you wake up, list things you want to say no to. Identify the obvious tasks you want to avoid.

- 🙅 Take a break, then return to your retreat space and expand your "say no" list. Review requests, appointments, volunteer work and commitments for the coming days, weeks and months. Note the tasks you want to decline, and why.

- 🙅 After another break, review your list and start saying no. Start with a small win, like crossing off a demanding task. Next, focus on the tougher rejections that may involve saying no to someone you care about or work with.

articles.headline: Spain train crash leaves at least 64 dead in second major collision this year
keyFacts: At least 64 people died and 58 were injured when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, according to regional officials.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the crash happened because a Renfe train was authorized to proceed past a red signal, breaking protocol.
Emergency services responded to the scene, and political parties briefly paused their election campaigning following the disaster.
body: BARCELONA, Spain — At least 64 people were killed and 58 injured when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, sending carriages careering off the tracks, in the second major accident on the same line in less than a year.

“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail,” one passenger, Miguel, told Spain’s COPE radio, adding that he was traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains.
“Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train — I imagine it must have been the other one,” he added.

Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo.
As rescue teams continued to search through the wreckage of the derailed carriages, the Castilla-La Mancha regional government said 64 people had been killed and 58 injured.
Earlier, the region’s President Emiliano García-Page said that at least 80 people were injured. Together the two trains were carrying more than 500 passengers.

Spain’s transport minister Oscar Puente said the crash occurred after a state-owned Renfe high-speed train was authorised to continue its journey despite an active red signal because of a stationary train from private rail company Iryo on the tracks ahead.

Addressing reporters in Madrid, Puente said the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure which automatically stopped traffic. An erroneous decision was made to restart the Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said.

Locals rushed to the scene of the accident, which has prompted a major national emergency response and raised questions about the safety and security of Spain’s high-speed rail infrastructure, which had previously been hailed as among the most sophisticated in Europe.

Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, told state broadcaster TVE that the trains were heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville when one ran into the tail of the other, which had stopped on the line.
She added that some 397 people had been traveling on the Renfe train and 147 people on the Iryo train.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was “deeply saddened” by the crash and said emergency services were working to assist those affected. “My heartfelt sympathy, solidarity, and support go out to all the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.
His sentiments were echoed by Spain’s royal family who said they shared “in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”

Spanish political parties said Wednesday they would briefly pause campaigning ahead of next month’s general election. Spain’s football federation also said it would postpone some of its Copa del Rey soccer fixtures, following the collision.
Juan Manuel Moreno, the president of the Andalusian regional government, said on X that there would be three days of mourning in the region.
The full scale of the disaster remains unclear but officials said an emergency phone line had been set up for families of the victims; local blood banks had also made appeals for donations.
Manuel Galan, the mayor of the nearby municipality of Urda, said he had been asked by emergency services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.
Train collision in Spain kills at least 30 people
Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Spain’s Cadena SER radio that she felt a strong impact that threw her forward and she initially thought the train had made an emergency stop.
After climbing down an embankment to safety, she said she saw part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage. “I saw dead people,” she added.
Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said.
The crash comes 10 months after a deadly collision in January between high-speed trains run by the same operators, Renfe and Iryo, on the same line between Madrid to Seville.
That accident left 45 people dead in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train.
The January crash was the country’s deadliest since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe for trains moving more than 155 mph, with more than 1,900 miles of track, according to the European Union.
